inline.s: Why? Subhuti! Because all bodhisattvas do not receive merit and virtue.”

—Why does the bodhisattva who “knows all dharmas are without self and attains the patient endurance” have such great merit and virtue? Subhuti! Because they do not receive merit and virtue. (This says: not receiving merit and virtue, being detached from marks, is precisely how merit and virtue are accomplished.)
In the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch
Chapter Three, on Resolving Doubts, there is a passage clarifying merit and virtue, translated as follows:

Prefect Wei said: Your disciple has heard that when Master Bodhidharma first converted Emperor Wu of Liang, the Emperor Wu asked: In my whole life I have built temples and ordained monks, given in charity and established vegetarian feasts—how much merit does this bring? Master Bodhidharma answered: In truth not the slightest merit. Your disciple does not understand this principle, and begs the Master to explain it for me.

The Sixth Patriarch said: Emperor Wu's building of temples, ordaining of monks, giving in charity, and establishing vegetarian feasts, though very extensive, truly brought not the slightest merit! Do not doubt the words of the former sages and think that Master Bodhidharma spoke wrongly. Emperor Wu held wrong views and did not know the right Dharma. Building temples, ordaining monks, giving in charity, and establishing vegetarian feasts—these are the cultivation of blessings; blessings must not be taken as merit and virtue. Merit and virtue are within the dharma-body, not in the cultivation of blessings. . . . Merit and virtue must be seen within the self-nature, and cannot be obtained by outward giving and offerings. Therefore blessings and merit and virtue are different. Emperor Wu did not understand the true principle of how to accomplish merit and virtue, and so though his good deeds were many, in truth there was no merit and virtue; it is not that our Patriarch spoke wrongly.
The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch
Chapter Seven, on Conditions, says: “When there is a self, offense is born; forgetting merit, blessings are beyond compare.”

Subhuti said to the Buddha: World-Honored One! How is it that a bodhisattva does not receive merit and virtue? Subhuti! The merit and virtue a bodhisattva creates should not be greedily clung to; therefore it is said that he does not receive merit and virtue.

Subhuti respectfully asked the Buddha: World-Honored One! Why does a bodhisattva not receive merit and virtue? The Buddha answered: Subhuti! The merit and virtue a bodhisattva creates should not be greedily craved or clung to; therefore it is said that he does not receive merit and virtue.

[The merit and virtue a bodhisattva creates should not be greedily clung to] Because all dharmas are ultimately empty, nothing whatsoever, unattainable. If one greedily clings to merit and virtue as obtainable, falsely grasping merit and virtue as truly existent, then there are the mark of a self, the mark of a human, the mark of a being, and the mark of a life, and that is not a bodhisattva.

The Song of Certifying the Way says: “Giving while clinging to marks brings heavenly blessings, like shooting an arrow straight into the sky; when its force is spent, the arrow falls back down, bringing a next life full of disappointment. How much better the gate of the unconditioned and true character, one leap straight into the Tathāgata's ground.” If a bodhisattva greedily clings to the merit and virtue he creates, he is turned by marks. Great Master Huiyuan's Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra says: “To renounce marks and enter the real is called right mindfulness.” As long as right mindfulness is not lost, carrying firewood and drawing water is practice; if right mindfulness is lost, then even sitting in meditation with eyes closed is not practice. Guard right mindfulness!

blocks.text: Chapter Twenty-nine: The Stillness of Deportment

inline.s: The World-Honored One feared that people might seek a Buddha with form and marks in the four deportments (walking, standing, sitting, and lying down), not knowing that the Buddha of the true nature is without marks, without coming or going, sitting or lying—the stillness of deportment.
Subhuti! If someone says that the Tathāgata comes, goes, sits, or lies down, such a person does not understand the meaning of what I have taught.
Subhuti! If someone says that the Tathāgata comes and goes, sits and lies down, such a person does not understand the meaning of the Tathāgata as I have taught it.

Master Yinshun writes in A Study of the Tathāgatagarbha: “In India in the age of Shakyamuni, regarding the continuation of beings' lives—coming from a former life into this life, and going from this life into a future life—it was already the common faith of the great majority. In the continuing on of beings, in birth and death, people always felt that there was something coming and going, and this too was called ‘thus-come’ or ‘thus-gone.’” So the World-Honored One here points out that the “Tathāgata” is not as people imagine—coming and going, sitting and lying down.
Why? The Tathāgata is without coming from anywhere and without going anywhere; therefore he is called the Tathāgata.
Why? Because the Tathāgata (the dharma-body) is utterly still and without marks, and so he neither comes nor goes; this is called the Tathāgata.
In the Great Prajñā-Pāramitā Sūtra

Volume Four Hundred, the Buddha says: “Good man! All Tathāgatas, worthy ones, perfectly enlightened ones cannot be seen by the form body. The Tathāgata is the dharma-body. Good man! The Tathāgata's dharma-body is the true suchness and dharma-realm of all dharmas; and since true suchness and the dharma-realm cannot be said to have coming or going, the Tathāgata's dharma-body is likewise without coming and without going.”

[Dharma-body] One of the Buddha's three bodies, the Buddha's true body. Also called the body of self-nature, or the body of dharma-nature, that is, the body of true suchness and dharma-nature realized by all Buddhas. Again: the dharma-body is the body of the dharma-nature that is originally present; whether a Buddha appears in the world or not, it constantly abides, unmoving, without change. Again: the dharma-body means that the Tathāgata's dharma-nature is true and constant, utterly still and pure, pervading the dharma-realm. The scripture says: the Buddha takes the Dharma as his body, pure as empty space; this is called the dharma-body. Again: the dharma-body refers to the right Dharma spoken by the Buddha, the outflow-free dharmas attained by the Buddha, and the Buddha's self-nature, true suchness, and tathāgatagarbha.

blocks.text: Chapter Thirty: The Mark of a Unity

inline.s: [The mark of a unity] “A unity” means that which is joined into one, like the modern phrase “a whole.” “The mark of a unity” is the unity-mark spoken of in this section.

Subhuti! If good men and good women ground a three-thousand-great-thousand world into minute dust-motes, what do you think, would that mass of minute dust-motes not be many? Subhuti said: Very many, World-Honored One! Why? If that mass of minute dust-motes were truly existent, the Buddha would not say it is a mass of minute dust-motes. Why is this? What the Buddha says is a mass of minute dust-motes is not a mass of minute dust-motes; therefore it is called a mass of minute dust-motes.
Subhuti! If good men and good women ground a three-thousand-great-thousand world into minute dust-motes, what do you think, would that mass of minute dust-motes not be many?”

—The World-Honored One asked: Subhuti! If good men and good women ground a three-thousand-great-thousand world into minute dust-motes, what do you think, would all these minute dust-motes not be many?

[Ground a three-thousand-great-thousand world into minute dust-motes] In modern terms: to break down a three-thousand-great-thousand world into elementary particles. [That mass of minute dust-motes] All these minute dust-motes. [Elementary particles] Elementary particles are the smallest and most basic units composing matter. But because human understanding of the composition of matter has gradually deepened, the content of “elementary particles” has also changed over time.

Subhuti said: Very many, World-Honored One! Why? If that mass of minute dust-motes were truly existent, the Buddha would not say it is a mass of minute dust-motes. Why is this? What the Buddha says is a mass of minute dust-motes is not a mass of minute dust-motes; therefore it is called a mass of minute dust-motes.”

—Subhuti answered: Very many indeed, World-Honored One! Why? If the mass of minute dust-motes were truly existent, the Buddha would not say it is a mass of minute dust-motes. Why is this? What the Buddha says is a mass of minute dust-motes (having marks) is not a mass of minute dust-motes (no substance); therefore it is called a mass of minute dust-motes (is illusion).

[If that mass of minute dust-motes were truly existent, the Buddha would not say it is a mass of minute dust-motes. Why is this? What the Buddha says is a mass of minute dust-motes is not a mass of minute dust-motes; therefore it is called a mass of minute dust-motes.] If elementary particles were truly existent, the Buddha would not say these elementary particles are many. Why is this said? Because what the Buddha says is elementary particles being many is not elementary particles being many; therefore it is called elementary particles being many. This says that elementary particles are illusion.

This says: not only are all objects illusion, but the elementary particles composing these objects are also illusion. By the world's traditional way of thinking, a tall building is real and a mirage is illusion; yet in fact the dust, water vapor, and light composing a mirage are of the same nature of existence as the steel and concrete of a tall building. If the tall building is said to be real, then the dust, water vapor, and light composing the mirage should also be real. So the World-Honored One analyzes deeply and says: not only is the three-thousand-great-thousand world illusion, but the basic units composing these illusions of the three-thousand-great-thousand world are also illusion.

[Mirage] A false image formed when light reflected by objects on the earth is refracted by the atmosphere; the so-called mirage is an optical illusion. The “shen” is a legendary sea-monster said to be able to breathe out vapor that forms the shapes of towers and terraces.

World-Honored One! What the Tathāgata says is a three-thousand-great-thousand world is not the world; therefore it is called the world. Why? If the world were truly existent, it would be a unity-mark. What the Tathāgata says is a unity-mark is not a unity-mark; therefore it is called a unity-mark.

Subhuti continued: World-Honored One! What the Tathāgata says is a three-thousand-great-thousand world (having marks) is not the world (no substance); therefore it is called the world (is illusion). (This says the three-thousand-great-thousand world is an illusion.) Why? If the three-thousand-great-thousand world were truly existent, then it would be a unity-mark. What the Tathāgata says is a unity-mark is not a unity-mark; therefore it is called a unity-mark.

In “Chapter Thirteen, on Receiving and Upholding in Accord with the Dharma,” the World-Honored One had clearly already told Subhuti that the world is illusion: “The Tathāgata says the world is not the world; therefore it is called the world.” Why does he still say “if the world were truly existent”? Because although Subhuti had already realized that “all marks whatsoever are false and vain,” he wanted to inquire further into “that which is truly existent,” that is, where the dream of ignorance ends; and so he says, “If the world were truly existent, it would be a unity-mark,” and deliberately continues the format “the Tathāgata says . . . is not . . . therefore it is called . . . ,” adding the line “What the Tathāgata says is a unity-mark is not a unity-mark; therefore it is called a unity-mark,” to see how the World-Honored One would comment on and teach about this “truly existent.”
Subhuti! A unity-mark is inexpressible; yet ordinary people greedily cling to the matter.

The World-Honored One told Subhuti: The “unity-mark” you speak of far exceeds thought, imagination, and verbal expression; it is inexpressible. Yet ordinary people greedily cling to the matter, always wanting to figure it out.

Concerning this ultimate question, the World-Honored One teaches in the Complete Enlightenment Sutra: “Good man! The realm perfected by the hearers—body, mind, and language are all utterly cut off—still cannot reach the nirvāṇa manifested by their own personal realization; how much less can one, with a thinking mind, fathom the Tathāgata's realm of perfect enlightenment—like taking a firefly's flame to burn Mount Sumeru, it can never set it alight. To enter the Tathāgata's great sea of still extinction with a mind of birth and death and views of birth and death can never reach it. Therefore I say that all bodhisattvas and the beings of the last age must first cut off the root of beginningless birth and death.”
Therefore, to understand the truly existent unity-mark, one must first cut off the root of beginningless birth and death—ignorance.

[A unity-mark is inexpressible] The truly existent unity-mark cannot be expressed in words or imagined by the mind. [Yet ordinary people greedily cling to the matter] Yet ordinary people recklessly conjecture and discuss it. Because the thinking of ordinary people is illusion, how can illusory thinking be used to know that which is truly existent? Hence the Complete Enlightenment Sutra says: “Thinking is itself illusory transformation; how much more so when one interrogates the false and vain. If one can understand this mind, then one may seek perfect enlightenment.”

Question: The unity-mark should be understood as “a collection of minute dust-motes.” The Great Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sutra says: “A unity-mark is so called because many conditions come together. Gathering many dust-motes to form form, and joining the five aggregates and so on to form a person, is called a unity-mark.”

Answer: The unity-mark should not be understood as “a collection of minute dust-motes.” For this section's scripture, Master Xuanzang's translation (Great Prajñā-Pāramitā Sūtra, Volume Five Hundred Seventy-seven) reads: “Furthermore, Good Manifestation. If a good man or good woman were to take the measure of the extremely minute dust-motes of the great earth of a three-thousand-great-thousand world, and out of worlds as numerous as that, with the forms and images of those countless worlds as ink, make a mass as of extremely minute dust-motes—Good Manifestation, what do you think? Would that mass of extremely minute dust-motes not be many? Good Manifestation answered: That mass of extremely minute dust-motes is very many, World-Honored One; very many, Well-Gone One. Why? World-Honored One, if that mass of extremely minute dust-motes were truly existent, the Buddha should not say it is a mass of extremely minute dust-motes. Why is this? What the Tathāgata says is a mass of extremely minute dust-motes is not a mass; therefore it is called a mass of extremely minute dust-motes. What the Tathāgata says is a three-thousand-great-thousand world is not the world; therefore it is called a three-thousand-great-thousand world. Why? World-Honored One, if the world were truly existent, it would be a unity-clinging; and what the Tathāgata says is a unity-clinging is not clinging; therefore it is called a unity-clinging. The Buddha said: Good Manifestation, this unity-clinging cannot be spoken, cannot be idly discussed; yet all those foolish ordinary beings and diverse-born ones forcibly cling to this dharma.” In this translation, what is called “a mass of minute dust-motes” is named “a mass of extremely minute dust-motes,” and “unity-clinging” is what Master Kumarajiva translated as “unity-mark.” From this we know that the unity-mark should not be understood as “a collection of minute dust-motes.”

[Well-Gone One] One of the Tathāgata's ten titles. “Well” means good; “gone” means departed. The Buddha cultivated the right Way, entered nirvāṇa, and departed toward a good destination; therefore he is titled “Well-Gone One.” [Diverse-born] Another name for ordinary beings, because ordinary beings turn through the six paths and are born receiving various and differing karmic results.

blocks.text: Chapter Thirty-one: The Non-Arising of Knowing and Seeing

inline.s: The non-arising of knowing and seeing” means not falsely clinging to the dharma of the Way as real, further breaking the self of dharmas. The Surangama Sutra
Volume Five says: “When knowing and seeing set up a knowing, that is the root of ignorance; when knowing and seeing are without seeing, that is nirvāṇa.”

Subhuti! If someone says that the Buddha speaks of the view of a self, the view of a human, the view of a being, and the view of a life. Subhuti! What do you think, does such a person understand the meaning of what I have taught? No, World-Honored One! Such a person does not understand the meaning of what the Tathāgata has taught. Why? What the World-Honored One says are the view of a self, the view of a human, the view of a being, and the view of a life are not the view of a self, the view of a human, the view of a being, and the view of a life; therefore they are called the view of a self, the view of a human, the view of a being, and the view of a life.

The World-Honored One said: Subhuti! If someone says that the Buddha speaks of the view of a self, the view of a human, the view of a being, and the view of a life, and therefore there truly are the view of a self, the view of a human, the view of a being, and the view of a life. Subhuti! What do you think? Does such a person understand the meaning of what I have taught? Subhuti answered: World-Honored One! Such a person does not understand the meaning of what the Tathāgata has taught. Why? What the World-Honored One says are the view of a self, the view of a human, the view of a being, and the view of a life refer to the illusion of the view of a self, the view of a human, the view of a being, and the view of a life, and do not say that such things truly exist.
In the Buddha Treasury Sutra

Chapter Three, on Mindfulness of Dharma, the Buddha says: “The sages and worthies do not form the thought: this is right view, this is wrong view. Why? Because all views arise from false conditions. Shariputra! If one forms the thought that this is right view, that person is holding wrong view. Shariputra, in the sage's dharma one uproots the foundation of all views and cuts off all paths of language, as in empty space where the hand touches nothing; all the dharmas of renunciants should be like this.”
[As in empty space where the hand touches nothing] As in empty space, where nothing at all can be touched. [Touching and obstruction] “Touch” is to touch; “obstruction” is to block.

The Buddha says: “Shariputra! The anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi of all Buddhas is only one meaning: detachment. What is detachment? Detachment from all desires and all views. Desire is ignorance, and view is recollection. Why? All dharmas have recollection as their root; whatever thought or notion there is, that is a view, and a view is wrong. Shariputra! Even a view within the good dharmas I also call a wrong view. Why? Shariputra! In detachment from desire and still extinction there is no dharma and no non-dharma, no good and no evil; all these matters are empty, far removed from all knots and all recollection; therefore it is called detachment.” (The Buddha Treasury Sutra
Chapter Seven, on Past Ages)

The layman Jiang Weannong's Lectures on the Diamond Sutra says: “You should know that the marks of the four marks are in fact nothing but the one mark of a self. And the root of the mark of a self in fact arises from the view of a self.” This says that the view of a self is the root of ignorance. In the Complete Enlightenment Sutra the Buddha says: “What is ignorance? Good man! All beings, from beginningless time, have various inversions, like a deluded person who mistakes the four directions for one another, falsely taking the four great elements as the mark of their own body and the conditioned shadows of the six dusts as the mark of their own mind. It is like a diseased eye seeing flowers in the sky and a second moon. Good man! In the sky there truly are no flowers; the diseased one falsely clings to them, and because of this false clinging he is not only deluded about the self-nature of this emptiness but also deluded about where the real flowers arise. From this false existence he turns through birth and death; therefore it is called ignorance.”
Subhuti! Those who arouse the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should, toward all dharmas, thus know, thus see, thus believe and understand, without giving rise to the mark of dharmas.

Subhuti! Those who arouse the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should, toward all dharmas of the Way, know, regard, believe, and understand in this way (referring to the above: the four views are illusion): neither non-existent nor existent, but illusion.
[Without giving rise to the mark of dharmas] Not clinging to the marks of the dharma of the Way and taking them as real.

Of this passage of scripture, the Lectures on the Diamond Sutra comments: “That is to say, the bodhisattva who has aroused the great mind should thus know, see, believe, and understand. From the opening of the sutra, all that has been said—arousing the vast mind, undertaking the vast practice, not grasping the marks of dharmas or non-dharmas, and even arousing the mind without dwelling, expounding the Dharma without dwelling, attaining the fruit without dwelling, and not dwelling even in non-dwelling—is nothing but causing one to know, see, believe, and understand thus and thus. For only by thus knowing, seeing, believing, and understanding does one comprehend the dharma of no-self. Therefore it says: one should thus know, see, believe, and understand.”
Question: “Dharmas” means all things and phenomena; why is “dharmas” here interpreted as “the dharma of the Way”?

Answer: The word “dharmas” has several meanings: first, all things and phenomena; second, the dharma of the Way (the dharma of becoming a Buddha); third, the dust of dharmas. The core of this sutra is to break clinging to the four marks (self, human, being, life) and to the mark of dharmas—what is called “cutting off ordinary sentiment, casting out sage understanding (even enlightenment is spat out).” The content of this section is the casting out of sage understanding, thoroughly breaking the self of dharmas (one must not falsely cling to the dharma of the Way as real, thinking there is a dharma to cultivate, a Way to accomplish, a fruit to realize); and the “dharmas” spoken of in the sixth and seventh sections—“no mark of dharmas, and no mark of non-dharmas,” “one should not grasp at dharmas, nor grasp at non-dharmas,” “non-dharmas, not non-dharmas”—also all mean the dharma of the Way. Therefore, according to the sutra's meaning and the context, “dharmas” here means the dharma of the Way. Master Jiazang's Commentary on the Humane King Sutra

Two says: “Emptiness breaks the five aggregates; emptiness-of-emptiness breaks emptiness. It is like taking medicine that can cure a disease: once the disease is cured, the medicine too should be expelled. If the medicine is not expelled, then it becomes the disease again. Using emptiness to break the disease of afflictions, one fears that emptiness will in turn become a trouble. Therefore one uses emptiness to relinquish emptiness; this is called emptiness-of-emptiness.” The meaning is: use medicine to cure disease; once the disease is cured, one should stop taking the medicine—if one keeps taking it, it is still harmful. This clarifies: use sage understanding to cut off ordinary sentiment; once ordinary sentiment is cut off, one should discard sage understanding. Concretely: use the principle of emptiness (the medicine) to break clinging to the five aggregates (form, feeling, perception, formation, consciousness) (the disease)—this is cutting off ordinary sentiment; once clinging to the five aggregates is broken, if one still clings to the principle of emptiness and will not let go, this is crossing the river without abandoning the raft, still lingering on the bank, and one cannot reach the treasure isle (cannot wake from the dream of ignorance). Therefore one must empty out even the principle of emptiness (realize that the principle of emptiness is also empty—is illusion, not to be clung to; that is emptiness-of-emptiness). Cut off ordinary sentiment (break the clinging to persons), discard sage understanding (break the clinging to dharmas).

All dharmas are false and originally empty and still; when all views do not arise, there is no mark of self, human, being, or life. Master Dixian says: “What is known is originally no obstruction; the Way lies simply in not clinging. Deluded thoughts need not be removed; the Way lies simply in not being turned by them.” The Buddhas, within the manifest arising and ceasing, see only the non-arising; beings, within the utterly still non-arising, see only arising and ceasing. Awakened, then arising and ceasing are all non-arising; deluded, then the non-arising is all arising and ceasing. Once one sees through all dharmas as illusion, conditions no longer drag the mind, love and hate have no way to arise, and one will no longer be deluded and create karma.

All dharmas are illusion, and the dharma of the Way that one upholds is also illusion. Working on in this way, breaking illusion layer by layer like peeling a banana tree, when one breaks through to the utmost point, the great dream awakens!

Marks are born from thought, and thought is born from view. Hence the ancients said: no need to seek the true; one need only still the views. If knowing and seeing dissolve, what is not true? Detachment from views is the ultimate principle for leaving birth and death and realizing the dharma-body. Master Ashvaghosha showed people that detachment from thought is true cultivation and true realization. Since view gives rise to thought (because thought comes from view), if the view fades then thought is detached of itself, and delusion is naturally extinguished. Therefore detachment from view is of the utmost importance. Let the chest be emptied out, open and bare, keeping not the slightest knowing and seeing as master. When knowing and seeing do not remain, the true seeing shines forth. (See Great Master Hanshan: The Dream Wandering Collection
Addressed to the Master of the Six-Fold Ease Retreat)
Detached from marks, detached from thought, detached from view. Detachment from view is the most ultimate and most fundamental.
Subhuti! What is spoken of as the mark of dharmas, the Tathāgata says is not the mark of dharmas; therefore it is called the mark of dharmas.
Subhuti! What is called the mark of dharmas, the Tathāgata says is not real, but illusion.

In the fourteenth section, “the Tathāgata says that all marks are not marks” means that all things and phenomena are illusion; the mark of dharmas here means the dharma of the Way, that is, as said at the end of the eighth section, the dharma of the Way is also illusion (an affair within the dream of ignorance), thoroughly breaking the clinging to dharmas.
The main body of the sutra ends here.

blocks.text: Chapter Thirty-two: Response-Bodies Are Not True

inline.s: To expound this sutra for others is to respond to beings' capacities and conditions and so liberate them; this affair too is illusion, and one must not cling to marks. Hence it is said that “response-bodies are not true.” This section is the circulation portion.

Subhuti! If someone took the seven treasures filling measureless asaṃkhyeya worlds and gave them away; and if good men and good women who have aroused the bodhi mind held to this sutra, even a four-line verse, received, upheld, read, and recited it, and expounded it for others, their merit surpasses the former.

Subhuti! If someone gave in charity the seven treasures filling measureless asaṃkhyeya (countless) worlds; and if again good men and good women who have aroused the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi held to this sutra, even a four-line verse, received, upheld, read, and recited it, and expounded it for others, their merit surpasses the former.
[Arouse the bodhi mind] The abbreviation of arousing the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Concerning giving the seven treasures, this was explained in the earlier scriptures. In “Chapter Eight, on the Birth of All in Accord with the Dharma”: if a person filled a three-thousand-great-thousand world with the seven treasures and gave them away. In “Chapter Eleven, on the Merit of the Unconditioned Being Supreme”: giving the seven treasures of a three-thousand-great-thousand world multiplied by the sands of the Ganges. Here it is giving the seven treasures filling measureless asaṃkhyeya three-thousand-great-thousand worlds, a number far, far greater still.

The scriptures of this sutra must be awakened to in practice (receiving, upholding, reading, reciting, and expounding for others) and practiced within awakening—this is to uphold the Diamond Sutra, and its karmic reward is inconceivable.
What does the Diamond Sutra teach? It teaches:

“All marks whatsoever are false and vain. If one sees all marks as no marks, one sees the Tathāgata.” “No mark of a self, no mark of a human, no mark of a being, no mark of a life.” “No mark of dharmas, and no mark of non-dharmas.” “All bodhisattvas and great bodhisattvas should thus give rise to the pure mind: they should not give rise to a mind dwelling in form, nor give rise to a mind dwelling in sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas; they should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere.” “Detached from all marks, one is named a Buddha.” “I should liberate all beings, and when all beings have been liberated, not one being has in fact been liberated.” “Not grasping at marks, abiding in the unmoving thusness.” “All conditioned dharmas are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, like dew and also like lightning; they should be contemplated thus.”

Hold these few scriptural lines firmly in mind, and at all times contemplate and examine them, not being turned by conditions—this is to receive and uphold the Diamond Sutra. (The reason one is turned by conditions is that one has taken as real the marks that are all false and vain.)
[Contemplation] To observe matters, principles, and all dharmas with wisdom, and to illuminate and understand them clearly.
Question: The World-Honored One says:

“If someone took the seven treasures filling measureless asaṃkhyeya worlds and gave them away; and if good men and good women who have aroused the bodhi mind held to this sutra, even a four-line verse, received, upheld, read, and recited it, and expounded it for others, their merit surpasses the former.”
And earlier he also said:
“If good men and good women give in charity their bodies as many times as the sands of the Ganges in the first portion of the day
(one grain of sand is a simile for one life)

, and again in the middle portion of the day give in charity their bodies as many times as the sands of the Ganges, and in the latter portion of the day also give in charity their bodies as many times as the sands of the Ganges
(three times a day)

, thus giving their bodies for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas; and if again someone hears this sutra and has faith without opposition, that person's merit surpasses the former—how much more so one who writes it out, receives, upholds, reads, and recites it, and explains it for others.” “I recall that in past ages, countless asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, before Dipankara Buddha, I met eight hundred forty million billion nayuta Buddhas, and served and made offerings to them all, without passing by a single one; if again someone, in a later age of decline, can receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, the merit he obtains—compared with the merit of my offerings to all those Buddhas—does not come to one hundredth of his, nor to one thousand ten-thousand millionth of his, indeed not to any fraction expressible by reckoning or simile.”
Why is the merit and virtue obtained by receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting the Diamond Sutra and expounding it for others so exceedingly great?

Answer: The self-nature of beings is no different from the Buddha's; their merit and virtue are originally perfect and complete, beyond all measure. Yet beings are deluded, like a billionaire who has lost his memory in a foreign land: he forgets that he has countless gold, silver, and treasures at home, and goes out to work for a living. How can the little money earned by working compare with the countless treasures at home? Therefore the Sixth Patriarch Huineng said:
“Not apart from the self-nature—that is the field of blessing.”
To receive, uphold, read, and recite the Diamond Sutra and expound it for others is to unfold the merit and virtue inherent in our self-nature; of course they are this great! The Lotus Sutra
Chapter Eight, on the Prophecy to Five Hundred Disciples, says:
“Suppose a person went to the house of a close friend and, drunk, lay down. At that time the friend had official business and had to go out
(his friend had to leave at once on official business)

. He tied a priceless pearl in the lining of his garment, gave it to him, and left. The man, drunk and asleep, was altogether unaware. After rising he wandered on to another country. For the sake of food and clothing he sought with diligence and great hardship. If he gained a little, he thought it was enough. Later the friend happened to meet him and said: ‘Foolish man, why do you seek food and clothing to such a degree? I once wished to give you peace and happiness, with the five desires freely enjoyed; on a certain year, month, and day I tied a priceless pearl in the lining of your garment. It is still there now, yet you do not know it, and toil and worry to keep yourself alive—how foolish! Now you can trade this treasure for whatever you need, and it will always be as you wish, with nothing lacking.’”
How should one expound it for others? Not grasping at marks, abiding in the unmoving thusness.
(Question:) How should one expound it for others? (Answer:) Not grasping at marks, abiding in the unmoving thusness.

How should one expound it for others?” This is a question, and it contains two meanings. First, it asks how the one who expounds should himself expound. Second, it asks what should be expounded for the listeners. Therefore the answer, “not grasping at marks, abiding in the unmoving thusness,” also contains two meanings. First, the one who expounds should “not grasp at marks, abide in the unmoving thusness”—that is, when expounding for others, he himself must not cling to marks. He teaches by his own example, and example outweighs words. At the very beginning of this sutra, the World-Honored One was expounding in just this way, and Subhuti saw through it and praised it as rare. Second, as for the listeners, one should tell them that all marks whatsoever are false and vain, that they should not grasp at marks but abide in the unmoving thusness—that is, tell them to be detached from marks.

[Not grasping at marks, abiding in the unmoving thusness] Not clinging to marks as real (the sutra says, “all marks whatsoever are false and vain”) and being entangled by them. That is: not clinging to marks, not stirring the mind. [Thusness] Thus in true suchness. This is the self-nature's realm of equal non-duality, free of inverted discrimination. [True suchness] True is the true mark, thus is so; the true mark is so; therefore it is called “true suchness,” that is, the true character of all dharmas.
Not grasping at marks, abiding in the unmoving thusness”

(inwardly not turned by thoughts, outwardly not dragged by conditions)—this is the line that puts the finishing touch on the whole work! This is what the World-Honored One demonstrated for us at the very beginning of this sutra, from putting on his robe and taking up his bowl to spreading his seat and sitting down; and this is what the Elder Subhuti praised as rare. Now we understand the essential purport of the Diamond Sutra: detachment from illusion—not grasping at marks, abiding in the unmoving thusness.
Not grasping at marks”

—if, meeting a condition (outer or inner), the mind is moved and there is a sense of love and hate, liking and disliking, this is “grasping at marks.” When the Buddha awakened to the Way on the eighth day of the twelfth month, seeing the morning star, he said:
“How wondrous! All beings are complete with the Tathāgata's wisdom and virtue marks. Only because of deluded thought, inversion, and clinging do they fail to realize it.”

And deluded thought, inversion, and clinging all come from “grasping at marks” (taking illusion as real). Therefore, when meeting conditions, one should not grasp, not be defiled, not think; in every matter and every place, diligently examine—then one's practice strikes the vital point.
Abiding in the unmoving thusness”

—that is, to abide peacefully in the principle of true suchness, seeing within the manifest arising and ceasing only the non-arising, inwardly perfuming ignorance. Here the World-Honored One sets forth the unconditioned dharma: not grasping at marks, abiding in the unmoving thusness.
Not grasping at marks, abiding in the unmoving thusness”

, that is, being detached from marks and turning the light back to illuminate the pure self-nature—what is called “dismissing marks and contemplating the nature.” In the Surangama Sutra the Buddha says:

“You should know that all beings, from beginningless time, have continued in birth and death, all because they do not know the permanently abiding true mind, the pure, luminous essence of the nature, but use deluded thoughts; and because these thoughts are not true, there is turning about.”
The Surangama Sutra says:
“All beings, from beginningless time, have continued in birth and death, all because they do not know the permanently abiding true mind, the pure, luminous essence of the nature
(all because they do not know the pure, luminous essence of the nature that permanently abides in the true mind)
, but use deluded thoughts
(and instead use deluded thoughts)
; and because these thoughts are not true, there is turning about.”

[The true mind, the pure, luminous essence of the nature] The pure and luminous essence of the nature, the originally pure and wondrously luminous substance of the nature. Grammatically, “pure, luminous essence of the nature” is an appositive modifying the noun “true mind.” [Turning about] Segmentary birth and death and transformational birth and death. [Segmentary birth and death] For beings within the three realms and six paths, because of good and evil karma, their life spans all have limits and their bodies all have distinctions; therefore their birth and death is called “segmentary birth and death.” One who has ended segmentary birth and death escapes the turning about of rebirth. [Transformational birth and death] For sages of the three vehicles who have cut off the delusions of views and thoughts and ended segmentary birth and death, in the course of cultivating the Way deluded thoughts gradually cease and realization gradually increases; each period of this shift from delusion to awakening differs, and the passage from the earlier period into the later is just like one birth and death, its transformation wondrous and unfathomable, inconceivable; therefore it is called “transformational birth and death.” One who has ended transformational birth and death perfectly realizes the Buddha-fruit.
Question: How does one accomplish “not grasping at marks, abiding in the unmoving thusness”?

Answer: On this, Mr. Jiang Weannong's Lectures on the Diamond Sutra has a penetrating discussion. The Lectures say: “Surveying the scriptural passage quoted above (‘not grasping at marks, abiding in the unmoving thusness’), one may clearly understand that to be aware and illuminate directly at the place of non-arising is the wondrous method for removing ignorance. What is the place of non-arising? It is when no thought has yet arisen. When thought has not even arisen, what can be called a mark? What grasping could there be? If one can be thus closely and without interruption, then regarding non-grasping one will naturally have a hold. In sum, on the one hand, toward the unmoving place one gathers the mind in aware illumination, to accomplish non-grasping; on the other hand, when meeting conditions, one firmly holds to non-grasping (at marks), to perfect the unmoving. Then one may find an entry into the essence of thusness.”

It also says: “In sum: abiding in the unmoving thusness is the meaning of non-arising; not grasping at marks is the meaning of non-dwelling. One must first be aware of and illuminate the originally non-arising, and only then can one dwell nowhere. When one reaches dwelling nowhere at all, one realizes non-arising. Alternating the two in practice is the essential gate. Moreover, practicing in this way carries through to the very end. From the first step, up to the stages of abiding, practice, dedication, the grounds, equal enlightenment, and wondrous enlightenment (the fifty-two stages through which an ordinary being passes to Buddhahood: the ten stages of faith, the ten stages of abiding, the ten stages of practice, the ten stages of dedication, the ten grounds, equal enlightenment, and wondrous enlightenment), none goes beyond this. Therefore it is said: ‘Detached from all marks, one is named a Buddha.’”

It also says: “However, the method of beginning must be to be aware and illuminate from the place where no thought has stirred, that is, to contemplate the unmoving thusness of the original nature. This is the Surangama's meaning of taking the non-arising and non-ceasing as the cause of cultivation, and also the meaning of relying on the originally still nature to cultivate cessation and thereby attain concentration, and relying on the originally illuminating nature to cultivate contemplation and thereby attain wisdom. If one does not know to begin from here, one's practice is confused and disordered, blind cultivation and blind refinement. It is like boiling sand to make rice—it can never be done. Though the beginner is wholly ignorant, and contemplates without seeing, he must still deeply understand this principle and diligently practice perfect illumination. As said before, when the former thought has ceased and the latter thought has not yet arisen, at just such a time the one mind is utterly still, clear and bright—this is called illumination. ‘Perfect’ means neither exerting force nor not exerting force, neither sinking nor floating. This is the single thread of wisdom-light, the most initial skillful means of knowing illusion and at once being detached. On the other hand, one follows this verse and contemplates all dharmas as all like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, dew, and lightning—conditioned arising, immediately empty. This method is the most skillful of skillful means, what is called knowing illusion. It is best to cultivate both together, for the two methods mutually complete each other. For to be aware of and illuminate the original nature is to work at the source; to contemplate all dharmas is to work amid conditions and objects. Moreover, the former contemplation has more of the sense of cultivating concentration, and the latter contemplation has more of the sense of cultivating wisdom. Concentration can indeed give rise to wisdom, yet unless wisdom is first opened, that concentration cannot be accomplished. Therefore, in their mutual aid, the contemplation of conditioned arising is especially important, for by contemplating conditioned arising one can be drawn into the unmoving thusness. This meaning has been set forth in detail above. Consider the line ‘they should be contemplated thus’—it carries a strong sense of ‘nothing but this will do.’ How earnest! The word ‘contemplate’ is important: it means one should contemplate with the utmost intent.”
Why? All conditioned dharmas are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, like dew and also like lightning; they should be contemplated thus.

Why should one “not grasp at marks, abide in the unmoving thusness”? Because clinging to marks and dwelling is a conditioned dharma, and all conditioned dharmas are as false and unreal as a dream or illusion, as fleeting as a bubble or shadow, as momentary as morning dew or lightning; one should contemplate them thus (thus observe, realize, and examine amid all conditions and objects).
The Lectures on the Diamond Sutra says:

“‘All conditioned dharmas are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, like dew and also like lightning; they should be contemplated thus’—this is precisely showing that ‘abiding in the unmoving thusness’ should be entered by contemplating all dharmas as dreamlike and illusory. To make such contemplations as of dream and illusion is to dismiss the clinging of sentiment. These are all crucial keys within the sutra, not to be neglected.”

[Conditioned dharmas] Generally, dharmas produced by causes and conditions are called “conditioned dharmas”; dharmas not produced by causes and conditions are called “unconditioned dharmas.” Among the five positions and hundred dharmas, the first ninety-four dharmas are all conditioned dharmas with arising, ceasing, and change; only the last six dharmas are the pure, still, and extinct unconditioned dharmas. But in this sutra, judging from the context, clinging to marks as real is a conditioned dharma, and not clinging to marks as real is the unconditioned dharma.
The conditioned dharmas spoken of here are spoken in relation to the unconditioned dharma of the seventh chapter,
“all sages and worthies, by the unconditioned dharma, have their differences”
, and also in relation to the unconditioned dharma of the Sutra of Forty-Two Chapters. The Sutra of Forty-Two Chapters says:
“The Buddha said: To leave family and home, understand the mind and reach the root, and comprehend the unconditioned dharma is to be called a shramana.”
Mr. Jiang Weannong's Lectures on the Diamond Sutra says:

“What this sutra teaches is all unconditioned dharma. And it plainly says: ‘All sages and worthies, by the unconditioned dharma, have their differences.’ Yet now, when teaching expounding, receiving, and upholding, it has one contemplate conditioned dharmas
(like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, like dew and also like lightning)
. This is the greatest key to the whole sutra's purport, and likewise the crucial key for students of Buddhism.”

Therefore, judging from the echoes between the scriptural passages, the “conditioned dharmas” (seeking and clinging) of this section are spoken in relation to the “unconditioned dharma” of “Chapter Seven, on No Attainment and No Teaching,” and to the above “not grasping at marks, abiding in the unmoving thusness” (the unconditioned dharma). Here the World-Honored One, answering why one should “not grasp at marks, abide in the unmoving thusness” (the unconditioned dharma), says: because “all conditioned dharmas (seeking and clinging) are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, like dew and also like lightning; they should be contemplated thus.” (Scripture:

“How should one expound it for others? Not grasping at marks, abiding in the unmoving thusness. Why? All conditioned dharmas are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, like dew and also like lightning; they should be contemplated thus.”
) This is the World-Honored One's final reminder before concluding his teaching: be detached from marks!

In the seventh section it was said that “all sages and worthies, by the unconditioned dharma, have their differences,” and it was explained that the unconditioned dharma is cultivation detached from marks. Giving without dwelling in marks, without the mark of a self, the mark of a human, the mark of a being, or the mark of a life, without the mark of dharmas and also without the mark of non-dharmas—this is the unconditioned dharma. For example, in the third section the Buddha says, “Thus I liberate immeasurable, countless, boundless beings, and yet in truth not one being is liberated,” and in the fourth section the Buddha says, “giving without dwelling in marks”—these are the unconditioned dharma. In the Sutra of Forty-Two Chapters Spoken by the Buddha

“The Buddha said: The renunciant shramana cuts off desire and removes love, understands the source of his own mind, penetrates the Buddha's profound principle, and comprehends the unconditioned dharma. Within he obtains nothing, without he seeks nothing; the mind is not tied to the Way, nor does it bind karma; no thought, no doing, neither cultivating nor realizing. Without passing through the stages, he is naturally most honored; this is called the Way.”
Whereas
the conditioned dharma is cultivation clinging to marks. The Buddha says:
“If the bodhisattva's mind dwells in dharmas and so practices giving
(a conditioned dharma)
, it is like a man who enters the darkness and sees nothing. If the bodhisattva's mind does not dwell in dharmas and so practices giving
(the unconditioned dharma)
, it is like a man with eyes, illumined by the light of the sun, seeing all the various colors.”

(Chapter Fourteen) Here giving stands for the six perfections and ten thousand practices. The six perfections and ten thousand practices that cling to marks are conditioned dharmas; the six perfections and ten thousand practices detached from marks are the unconditioned dharma.

[All conditioned dharmas] In cultivating the Way one must above all avoid seeking and clinging. To cultivate while clinging to marks is to use illusion to enter illusion, and the wish to awaken only deepens delusion. The Complete Enlightenment Sutra says:

“Birth and death and nirvāṇa are like last night's dream. Good man! Because they are like last night's dream, you should know that birth and death and nirvāṇa are without arising and without ceasing, without coming and without going; what is realized has no gain and no loss, no grasping and no rejecting; the one who realizes has no doing and no stopping, no allowing and no extinguishing; within this realization there is neither subject nor object; ultimately there is no realization and also no realizer, and the nature of all dharmas is equal and indestructible.”

[Like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow] This says that clinging to marks and dwelling is like the illusion of a dream, like the shadow of a bubble—false and unreal; though at times it appears in all colors, it is soon destroyed. This is because cultivating while clinging to marks and dwelling obtains only human and heavenly blessings; and after obtaining blessings, one again does evil in reliance on them, falling all the deeper. Therefore the Yongjia Song of Certifying the Way says:

“Giving while clinging to marks brings heavenly blessings, like shooting an arrow straight into the sky; when its force is spent, the arrow falls back down, bringing a next life full of disappointment.”
The Sutra of the Great Vehicle's Contemplation of the Mind-Ground says:
“The thoughtless heavens live eighty thousand years; when blessings end they return to the evil paths, like a dream, an illusion, and a bubble, and like morning dew and lightning.”

[The thoughtless heavens live eighty thousand years] Master Taixu's Lectures on the Sutra of the Great Vehicle's Contemplation of the Mind-Ground says: “This is the heaven of neither perception nor non-perception in the formless realm. Eighty thousand years should be eighty thousand great kalpas.”

Therefore, on the bodhi path one must be detached from marks not only amid conditions and objects—“all marks whatsoever are false and vain”—but also in the dharma of the Way: “all conditioned dharmas are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow.” Breaking the two clingings, to persons and to dharmas, and with persons and dharmas both extinguished, one realizes the great Way.

Why should one “not grasp at marks, abiding in the unmoving thusness”—detached from marks and dwelling nowhere (the unconditioned dharma)? Because if one “receives, upholds, reads, and recites it and expounds it for others” while grasping at marks, that is clinging to marks and dwelling; and clinging to marks and dwelling is a conditioned dharma. All conditioned dharmas (clinging to marks and dwelling) are like a dream, an illusion, like a bubble, a shadow; though at times in all colors, they are soon destroyed, like morning dew or lightning, vanishing in a flash.

At the end of the work, the World-Honored One once more admonishes us with deep earnestness: by all means, do not cultivate while clinging to marks; cultivation that clings to marks is a conditioned dharma, “like a man who enters the darkness and sees nothing.” The conditioned dharma obtains only human and heavenly blessings; one cannot even leave the three realms, how much less realize the Buddha-fruit and wake from the great dream!
“Chapter Seven, on No Attainment and No Teaching” says:
“All sages and worthies, by the unconditioned dharma, have their differences.”
Great Master Yongjia made a striking contrast between the conditioned dharmas and the unconditioned dharma; the Song of Certifying the Way says:
Awakened, it is done, no effort applied; all conditioned dharmas are not the same.
Giving while clinging to marks
(a conditioned dharma)
brings heavenly blessings, like shooting an arrow straight into the sky.
When its force is spent, the arrow falls back down, bringing a next life full of disappointment.
How much better the gate of the unconditioned true character
(the unconditioned dharma)
, one leap straight into the Tathāgata's ground.
The Diamond Sutra is precisely the gate of the unconditioned true character, utterly perfect and utterly sudden, one leap straight into the Tathāgata's ground!

Therefore the key to liberation is to break all clinging and realize non-discriminating wisdom (also called realizing emptiness): not grasping at marks, abiding in the unmoving thusness. As for how to begin the work, how to contemplate, and how to be detached from marks, Mr. Jiang Weannong's Lectures on the Diamond Sutra explains it excellently:
“The Buddha spoke this sutra originally for ordinary beings who have aroused the great mind. These two lines
(‘not grasping at marks, abiding in the unmoving thusness’)
and this one verse
(‘all conditioned dharmas are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, like dew and also like lightning; they should be contemplated thus’)

precisely show the great-minded ordinary being where to begin the work. Therefore the two contemplations, before and after, must be practiced alternately, closely and without interruption. Practiced long, one will surely find an entry.
Since this unworthy one
(the humble way of saying “I”)

began to study Buddhism, for the first twenty years, though I practiced various methods and made various contemplations, I made no progress at all. One day, at these four lines I seemed suddenly to awaken, and practiced contemplation accordingly. At first it was as if near and as if far, as if clear and as if dim, not forming a continuous piece, and without much effect.
Then I realized that one should, amid all conditions and objects, exert the utmost intent to observe them

. Even in the smallest matter, or at times of the greatest smoothness or the greatest difficulty, one should seal it with the principle of dream and illusion; and even in practicing the Buddhadharma, seal it with the principle of dream and illusion
seal it

, in walking, standing, sitting, and lying, never apart from this. Thus for a long time, though my skill in ‘not grasping at marks, abiding in the unmoving thusness’ is still shallow, yet it truly began with making this contemplation. This mind gradually felt open and empty, and toward all conditions and marks it gradually became unmoved within. Reading the sutras, my eyes felt a little brighter; reciting the Buddha's name, I felt a little more steadfast. Now I ask you all to try it; you will surely have benefit. You should know that for an ordinary being of this lowly ground, wishing to turn the light back and illuminate, apart from this there is no place to begin. Treasure it! Treasure it!”

[The two contemplations, before and after] The contemplation of the unmoving original nature (the contemplation of the nature) and the contemplation of all dharmas as illusion (the contemplation of dream-illusion). The Lectures on the Diamond Sutra says:
However, the method of beginning must be to be aware and illuminate from the place where no thought has stirred, that is, to contemplate the unmoving thusness of the original nature
(the contemplation of the nature)

. This is the Surangama's meaning of taking the non-arising and non-ceasing as the cause of cultivation, and also the meaning of relying on the originally still nature to cultivate cessation and thereby attain concentration, and relying on the originally illuminating nature to cultivate contemplation and thereby attain wisdom. If one does not know to begin from here, one's practice is confused and disordered, blind cultivation and blind refinement. It is like boiling sand to make rice—it can never be done. Though the beginner is wholly ignorant, and contemplates without seeing, he must still deeply understand this principle and diligently practice perfect illumination. As said before, when the former thought has ceased and the latter thought has not yet arisen, at just such a time the one mind is utterly still, clear and bright—this is called illumination. ‘Perfect’ means neither exerting force nor not exerting force, neither sinking nor floating. This is the single thread of wisdom-light, the most initial skillful means of knowing illusion and at once being detached. On the other hand, one follows this verse and contemplates all dharmas as all like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, dew, and lightning—the very substance is immediately empty
(the contemplation of dream-illusion)

. This method is the most skillful of skillful means, what is called knowing illusion. It is best to cultivate both together, for the two methods mutually complete each other. For to be aware of and illuminate the original nature is to work at the source; to contemplate all dharmas is to work amid conditions and objects. Moreover, the former contemplation has more of the sense of cultivating concentration, and the latter contemplation has more of the sense of cultivating wisdom. Concentration can indeed give rise to wisdom, yet unless wisdom is first opened, that concentration cannot be accomplished. Therefore, in their mutual aid, the contemplation of dream-illusion is especially important, for by contemplating dharmas as dreamlike and illusory one can be drawn into the unmoving thusness.

[Dream, illusion, bubble, shadow, dew, lightning] As false and unreal as a dream or illusion, as fleeting as a bubble or shadow, as momentary as morning dew or lightning. [The very substance is immediately empty] Without waiting for analysis, directly realizing that the substance itself is originally empty and nothing. [Lowly ground (thin ground)] A low and inferior position, referring to the lowly position of an ordinary being.

Question: The “conditioned dharmas” in the verse refers to the conditioned dharmas of Bodhisattva Vasubandhu's (also translated as Bodhisattva Vasubandhu) Treatise on the Door of Understanding the Hundred Dharmas of the Great Vehicle—all things produced by the union of causes and conditions. Why not explain it that way?

Answer: Taken by itself, this verse is usually explained as referring to all things produced by the union of causes and conditions, and that is not wrong. But the Diamond Sutra teaches the true character of all dharmas; therefore not only are conditioned dharmas like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, but unconditioned dharmas (all things not produced by the union of causes and conditions) are also like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow. So the conditioned dharmas spoken of here are spoken in relation to the unconditioned dharma of the seventh chapter,
“all sages and worthies, by the unconditioned dharma, have their differences”
, and also in relation to the unconditioned dharma of the Sutra of Forty-Two Chapters.

The Treatise on the Door of Understanding the Hundred Dharmas of the Great Vehicle gathers all dharmas into one hundred kinds: the first ninety-four are conditioned dharmas, and the last six are unconditioned dharmas. If the “conditioned dharmas” of “all conditioned dharmas are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow” meant the conditioned dharmas of the Treatise on the Door of Understanding the Hundred Dharmas, then a problem would arise: are the unconditioned dharmas of the Treatise on the Door of Understanding the Hundred Dharmas also like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow?

The answer is: the unconditioned dharmas too are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow. That is to say, all dharmas are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow. The basis for saying this is that at the very beginning of the Treatise on the Door of Understanding the Hundred Dharmas of the Great Vehicle, Bodhisattva Vasubandhu says:
“As the World-Honored One said,
all dharmas
are without self.”
That is, all dharmas are empty, and all dharmas are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow—not merely conditioned dharmas. In the Smaller Prajñā-Pāramitā Sutra the Buddha says:
All dharmas
are like an illusion, a dream, an echo, a shadow, a mirage.”
In the Mahāyāna Laṅkāvatāra Sutra the Buddha says:
“The bodhisattva and great bodhisattva should teach that
all dharmas
are like an illusion, like a dream.”
[All dharmas are without self] All the ten thousand dharmas are illusion, and no inherent nature can be spoken of; this is called the non-self of dharmas, also called the emptiness of dharmas.

Since all dharmas are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, why does the Buddha here say only “all conditioned dharmas are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, like dew and also like lightning; they should be contemplated thus,” and not “all dharmas are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, like dew and also like lightning; they should be contemplated thus”? Therefore the conditioned dharmas spoken of here mean: clinging to marks as real is a conditioned dharma.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Elder Subhuti, and all the monks and nuns, the laymen and laywomen, and all the heavenly beings, humans, and asuras of every world, having heard what the Buddha said, were all greatly delighted, and believed, accepted, and practiced it.

When the World-Honored One had finished speaking this sutra, the Elder Subhuti, and all the monks and nuns, the laymen and laywomen, and all the heavenly beings, humans, and asuras of every world, having heard what the Buddha said, were all greatly delighted, and believed, accepted, and practiced it.

[Layman] Rendered in Chinese as “pure-faith scholar,” that is, a male lay disciple who at home draws near to and serves the Three Jewels and receives and upholds the five precepts. [Laywoman] Rendered in Chinese as “pure-faith woman,” that is, a female lay disciple who at home draws near to and serves the Three Jewels and receives and upholds the five precepts. [Believe, accept, and practice] To believe, to accept, and to practice as taught.

The great assembly's wisdom was suddenly opened, and they were filled with the joy of the Dharma—dissolving my deluded thoughts of a billion kalpas, without passing through asaṃkhyeya kalpas they attained the dharma-body.
[Asaṃkhyeya] Asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
All that the Diamond Sutra teaches throughout can be gathered into four questions: For what purpose? By what principle? What dharma is realized? What practice is cultivated?
1. For what purpose? To end the two deaths: to end segmentary birth and death and transformational birth and death.
2. By what principle? All dharmas are empty. At all times, closely apply the work of contemplation and examination, until one truly realizes that “all marks whatsoever are false and vain.”
